paper.title: Improvements in the GISTEMP Uncertainty Model

project.title: How Sure Are We That It Was the Hottest Year?
project.question: Using NASA's GISTEMP v4 global temperature record and its published uncertainty, how confident can we be that a given year was the warmest on record up to that date, and how does that confidence change as the record gets longer?
project.hypothesis: Because recent years have smaller uncertainty and are separated by a long-term trend, the probability that a recent record year is the true record will be high but below certainty, and it will be lower when the top years are close together.
data: GISTEMP v4 global annual mean anomalies (NASA GISS)
GISTEMP total uncertainty for the global annual mean (NASA GISS)
risks: Data files are updated every month; record the download date and version you used.
Treating each year's error as independent is a simplification; say so in your limitations.
Results describe the global record only; they say nothing about any single place.

guides.why: Read the temperature table, clean it and make plots.
guides.summary: pandas stores tables as DataFrames. You can read a CSV file while skipping title lines, mark symbols as missing values, select columns and filter rows by a condition, then plot the result.
steps: Read a CSV with skiprows and na_values
guides.practice: Load any small CSV with a title line and a missing-value symbol, and plot one column over time.

guides.why: GISTEMP reports differences from a reference period, not raw temperatures.
guides.summary: An anomaly is how much a value differs from an average over a chosen reference period. Climate records use anomalies because changes are more comparable across places than raw temperatures. Changing the baseline shifts all anomalies by the same amount but does not change trends.
steps: Compute an anomaly by subtracting a baseline mean
See that a new baseline shifts the curve but keeps its shape
Explain why stations are combined as anomalies
guides.practice: Take five daily temperatures, compute their mean, and write each day as an anomaly from that mean.

guides.why: You will measure how fast temperature changed over different periods.
guides.summary: A linear trend is the slope of the straight line that best fits the data. It summarizes the average rate of change over a period, but it depends on the period chosen and can hide changes in speed.
steps: Fit a straight line with numpy.polyfit
Read the slope and its units
Plot the data with the fitted line
guides.practice: Fit lines to the first half and the second half of any time series and compare the two slopes.

guides.why: You will simulate many possible histories from each year's uncertainty to estimate probabilities.
guides.summary: Uncertainty describes how far the true value might be from the reported one. Monte Carlo simulation draws many random versions of the data within that uncertainty, and the share of versions where something happens estimates its probability.
steps: Learn the normal distribution and standard deviation
Convert a 95% interval into a standard deviation
Count outcomes across simulations to estimate a probability
guides.practice: Simulate 10,000 rolls of two dice and estimate how often the sum is at least 10.
